description: Select metrics that inform decisions instead of measuring what is easy. Start with the decision the metric must inform. Then ask: what measurement would reduce uncertainty about that decision? The minimum measurement that reduces uncertainty is the right metric.

steps.description: Inventory the decisions that metrics must inform. A metric without a decision is decoration.

inputs.name: context
inputs.desc: What the metrics serve (a business, a product, a team, a personal goal)

inputs.name: time-horizon
inputs.desc: The planning horizon for the decisions

outputs.name: decision-list
outputs.desc: Every recurring decision with its frequency, current information used, and the uncertainty that makes it difficult

outputs.name: highest-uncertainty-decisions
outputs.desc: The 3-5 decisions where better information would produce the biggest improvement in decision quality

process: List every recurring decision: resource allocation, pricing, hiring, product direction, marketing channel selection, personal spending, health choices.
For each decision, identify the uncertainty: what do you not know that, if you knew it, would make the decision obvious?
Rank by impact: which decisions have the highest stakes multiplied by the highest uncertainty?
Select the top 3-5. These deserve dedicated metrics. Everything else uses existing data or periodic assessment.

steps.description: For each high-uncertainty decision, design the metric that reduces the uncertainty.

outputs.name: metric-definitions
outputs.desc: For each decision: the metric name, what it measures, how it is calculated, the data source, measurement frequency, and the threshold that triggers action

outputs.name: metric-limitations
outputs.desc: What each metric does NOT measure and the decisions it should NOT be used for

process: For each decision, ask: what single number, if you could see it updated in real time, would most reduce your uncertainty?
Define the metric precisely: name, calculation formula, data source, measurement frequency. Two people measuring independently should get the same number.
Set the action threshold: what metric value triggers a change in the decision?
Document the limitations: what does this metric NOT capture? Every metric is a proxy.

steps.description: Validate that the metric actually reduces decision uncertainty.

outputs.name: validation-results
outputs.desc: For each metric: does a change in value change the decision? Is it gameable? Is it timely?

outputs.name: final-metric-set
outputs.desc: The validated metrics with definitions, thresholds, and the decisions they inform

process: For each metric, run the thought experiment: if this metric moved to twice its current value, would you make a different decision? If neither doubling nor halving changes the decision, the metric is not useful.
Test for gaming: could someone improve the metric without improving the underlying reality?
Test for timeliness: by the time you see the metric, is it too late to act?
The final metric set should be 3-10 metrics total.

description: Design leading indicators that predict outcomes before they happen. Lagging indicators tell you what happened. Leading indicators tell you what will happen. Manage leading indicators and lagging indicators follow.

steps.description: Identify lagging indicators you care about and map the causal chain backward to find the behaviors that cause them.

inputs.name: goals
inputs.desc: The outcomes you want to improve

outputs.name: causal-chains
outputs.desc: For each outcome: the chain of causes from immediate driver to upstream behaviors, with the time delay at each link

outputs.name: candidate-leading-indicators
outputs.desc: Behaviors at the upstream end of each causal chain that predict the outcome

process: List the outcomes that matter. These are your lagging indicators.
For each, map backward: what directly causes this to move? What causes that cause? Continue until you reach behaviors you can directly influence.
Note the time delay at each link. Revenue lags pipeline by 30-90 days. Weight lags diet changes by 2-4 weeks.
The candidates are the behaviors at the actionable end: outbound activity, demos scheduled, calories consumed, workouts completed.

steps.description: Validate that the candidate leading indicators actually predict the lagging outcome.

outputs.name: validated-leading-indicators
outputs.desc: Indicators that pass: they predict the outcome with reasonable accuracy and lead time

outputs.name: leading-indicator-dashboard
outputs.desc: The final set with measurement definitions, targets, and the lagging indicators they predict

process: Test the correlation: using historical data, does the leading indicator move before the lagging indicator?
Test the direction: does more of the leading indicator cause the expected change in the lagging indicator?
Test actionability: can you directly influence the leading indicator?
Build the dashboard: leading indicators on the left (manage daily), lagging on the right (check monthly).

description: Design dashboards that inform decisions instead of decorating screens. Information hierarchy: the most important thing is largest and first. Three levels: summary (one glance), diagnostic (what changed), investigative (why it changed).

steps.description: Define who reads the dashboard, what decisions they make, and how often they look.

inputs.name: audience
inputs.desc: Who reads the dashboard and their role

inputs.name: decisions
inputs.desc: The decisions the dashboard must inform

outputs.name: dashboard-purpose
outputs.desc: The audience, decisions, cadence, and ranked information requirements

outputs.name: information-requirements
outputs.desc: The specific questions the dashboard must answer, ranked by importance

process: Identify the primary audience: executives (headline), managers (diagnosis), operators (detail).
List the decisions and the questions each decision needs answered.
Rank questions by importance. The most important gets the most prominent position.
Set the cadence: match it to the decision frequency.

steps.description: Build the three-level hierarchy: summary, diagnostic, investigative.

outputs.name: dashboard-layout
outputs.desc: The three levels: summary (1-3 headline numbers), diagnostic (breakdown charts), investigative (detail tables)

outputs.name: element-justifications
outputs.desc: For each element: the question it answers. Elements without a question are removed.

process: Summary level: 1-3 numbers visible at a glance. Large text, color coding, trend arrows. State visible in under 5 seconds.
Diagnostic level: breakdown by segment, time period, or category. Charts showing comparison.
Investigative level: detail tables, drill-downs. Only visible when the reader drills down.
Every element must answer a listed question. If it does not, remove it.

steps.description: Test with the actual audience. Can they answer their questions within the target time?

outputs.name: usability-results
outputs.desc: For each question: correctness, time to answer, confusion points

outputs.name: revised-dashboard
outputs.desc: The updated design incorporating findings

process: Show the dashboard to a target audience member. Ask them to answer each question out loud.
Measure: time to answer (summary under 10 seconds, diagnostic under 60 seconds), correctness, and confidence.
Note every confusion point: wrong chart, misread scale, unclear meaning.
Revise: fix confusion points, remove unused elements, enhance slow-to-read elements.

description: Design statistically valid A/B tests for any comparison. Define the minimum detectable effect, calculate sample size, set duration, define the stopping rule. No peeking at results before significance.

steps.description: Define the hypothesis and primary metric.

outputs.name: hypothesis
outputs.desc: The testable hypothesis with minimum detectable effect

outputs.name: primary-metric
outputs.desc: The single metric that determines the result

process: State the hypothesis: what do you expect to happen, and by how much?
Define the minimum detectable effect: the smallest improvement worth implementing.
Define the primary metric: one number, one decision. Testing multiple metrics inflates false positives.
Define the baseline: current metric value needed for sample size calculation.

steps.description: Calculate sample size needed for statistical confidence and translate to test duration.

outputs.name: required-sample-size
outputs.desc: Observations needed per variant at 95% confidence and 80% power

outputs.name: test-duration
outputs.desc: How long based on sample size and daily traffic

process: Calculate sample size per variant using the appropriate statistical formula for the metric type.
Key inputs: baseline rate, MDE, significance level (0.05), power (0.80).
Translate to duration: sample needed divided by daily traffic split between variants.
If duration exceeds 8 weeks: increase MDE or increase traffic. Do not shorten below required sample.

steps.description: Set execution rules: randomization, no peeking, stopping criteria.

outputs.name: execution-rules
outputs.desc: Randomization method, when results can be checked, stopping criteria

outputs.name: test-documentation
outputs.desc: Pre-registered test plan: hypothesis, metric, MDE, sample size, duration, rules

process: Randomize properly: each participant independently assigned. No alternating.
No peeking: do not check results before required sample size. Early peeking inflates false positives.
Only stop early for evidence of harm. Define the harm threshold before starting.
Document everything before the test starts. Pre-registration prevents after-the-fact rationalization.

steps.description: Analyze results and decide. Statistical significance is necessary but not sufficient.

outputs.name: result-analysis
outputs.desc: Observed effect, confidence interval, p-value, and significance determination

outputs.name: implementation-decision
outputs.desc: Implement (significant and meaningful), do not implement, or run follow-up

process: Calculate observed effect: difference between variants on the primary metric.
Calculate confidence interval. If it includes zero, the result is not statistically significant.
Check practical significance: is the effect large enough to justify implementation?
Decide: implement, skip, or follow up. Document the reasoning.

description: Group users or events by the moment that matters and track behavior over time. Cohort curves reveal what averages hide. An average retention of 50% could mean every cohort retains 50% or early cohorts retain 80% and recent cohorts retain 20%.

steps.description: Define the cohort grouping event, time window, and behavior metric.

outputs.name: cohort-definition
outputs.desc: The grouping event, time window (weekly, monthly), and behavior metric to track

outputs.name: cohort-table-structure
outputs.desc: Rows are cohorts by time window, columns are periods since grouping event, cells are the metric

process: Define the grouping event: sign-up date, first purchase, feature adoption date.
Define the time window: weekly (granular, small samples) or monthly (balanced).
Define the behavior metric: retention percentage, cumulative spending, sessions per week.
Build the table structure: cohorts as rows, age as columns, metric values as cells.

steps.description: Read the cohort curves: flattening (healthy), declining to zero (problem), or improving (ideal).

outputs.name: curve-analysis
outputs.desc: For each cohort: shape (flattening, declining, improving) and stabilization point

outputs.name: cohort-comparison
outputs.desc: Are recent cohorts improving, degrading, or stable vs. older ones?

process: Plot each cohort's curve over time. Look at shape, not just final number.
Flattening curve: remaining users are retained. Stabilization point is the long-term rate.
Declining to zero: leaky bucket. Where is the steepest drop? That is the intervention point.
Compare cohorts: newer better or worse? The trend reveals whether changes are working.

steps.description: Extract actionable insights: what to fix, what to repeat, where to intervene.

inputs.name: curve-analysis
inputs.desc: The curve shapes and stabilization points

outputs.name: actionable-insights
outputs.desc: Steepest drop period (intervention point), best cohort (what was different), and trend direction

outputs.name: recommended-actions
outputs.desc: Where to intervene, what to replicate, what to track going forward

process: Find the steepest drop: the highest-leverage intervention point.
Find the best cohort: what did they experience differently?
Find the trend: getting better or worse over time?
Recommend: intervene at the drop, replicate the best cohort, track monthly.

description: Set up anomaly detection: define normal, measure deviation, alert on significance. Catch real changes early, ignore noise. Works for any time-series metric.

steps.description: Establish the baseline: what is normal, accounting for trends, seasonality, and patterns.

inputs.name: metric-data
inputs.desc: Historical data (at least 30 data points, ideally 90+)

inputs.name: metric-description
inputs.desc: What the metric measures and known patterns

outputs.name: baseline-model
outputs.desc: Expected value for any given day with confidence band

outputs.name: normal-variability
outputs.desc: Typical fluctuation range: standard deviation, IQR, historical min/max

process: Collect 30+ data points. Identify patterns: trend, seasonality, day-of-week effect.
Build the baseline model: expected value for each day based on patterns.
Calculate normal variability: standard deviation of residuals (actual minus predicted).
This sets the threshold for what counts as an anomaly.

steps.description: Calibrate alert threshold: sensitive enough for real anomalies, tolerant enough against false alarms.

outputs.name: alert-thresholds
outputs.desc: Standard deviations from baseline for triggering (typically 2-3)

outputs.name: expected-false-positive-rate
outputs.desc: Expected false alarms per period at chosen threshold

process: Set initial threshold at 2 standard deviations. Catches 95% of real anomalies with 5% false alarm rate.
Backtest against historical data: how many alerts, how many were real?
Adjust based on backtest: too many false alarms = widen to 2.5 or 3. Missed real events = tighten.
Right threshold depends on cost of missing an anomaly vs. cost of investigating a false alarm.

steps.description: Define what happens when an alert fires: verify, investigate, classify, act or dismiss.

outputs.name: response-protocol
outputs.desc: Step-by-step: verify data, investigate cause, classify as real or false, take action or dismiss

outputs.name: anomaly-log-template
outputs.desc: Template for logging each alert with classification and action taken

process: Step 1: Verify the data. Is the metric value correct or is there a data collection error?
Step 2: Investigate the cause. Check for known events: deployments, campaigns, holidays, competitor actions.
Step 3: Classify. Real anomaly or false alarm? Update the log.
Step 4: Act (fix the problem or capitalize on the opportunity) or dismiss (note for threshold recalibration).

description: Determine which inputs caused the output. When multiple channels contribute to an outcome, attribution assigns credit. The model you choose determines where you invest next.

steps.description: Map every touchpoint in the path to conversion.

outputs.name: touchpoint-sequences
outputs.desc: Ordered sequences of touchpoints per conversion with timestamps and channels

outputs.name: touchpoint-summary
outputs.desc: Frequency of each channel by position (first, middle, last)

process: Collect all touchpoint data: web visits, ads, emails, social, calls, meetings, referrals.
Build the sequence for each conversion: ordered by timestamp with channel and campaign identified.
Summarize patterns: which channels appear most at first position (awareness), middle (nurture), last (conversion)?
Note data gaps: untraceable touchpoints (word of mouth, direct visits) create blind spots.

steps.description: Apply multiple attribution models and compare. Different models give different answers.

outputs.name: model-comparison
outputs.desc: Same data under 4 models (first-touch, last-touch, linear, time-decay) with credit distribution

outputs.name: selected-model
outputs.desc: The model that best fits the decision, with reasoning

process: First-touch: all credit to first touchpoint. Best for awareness investment decisions.
Last-touch: all credit to last touchpoint. Best for closing investment decisions.
Linear: equal credit to all. Best for understanding the full journey.
Time-decay: more credit to recent touchpoints. Best for overall budget allocation.
Select based on the decision: awareness = first-touch, closing = last-touch, budget = time-decay.

steps.description: Translate attribution results into investment decisions.

outputs.name: investment-recommendations
outputs.desc: For each channel: increase, decrease, or hold, based on attributed value per dollar

outputs.name: attribution-review-schedule
outputs.desc: When to re-run (quarterly) and when to reconsider the model (annually)

process: Calculate attributed value per dollar spent for each channel. Compare across channels.
High value per dollar = increase. Low value per dollar = decrease or investigate.
Before cutting: check the channel's role across models. A channel bad on last-touch might be essential on first-touch.
Set review schedule: re-run quarterly, re-evaluate model choice annually.

description: Audit data quality across five dimensions: completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, and uniqueness. Bad data in, bad decisions out. Fix the source, not the symptom.

steps.description: Score each critical data set across the five quality dimensions.

inputs.name: critical-data-sets
inputs.desc: Data sets that inform important decisions

inputs.name: quality-standards
inputs.desc: Minimum acceptable quality for each dimension

outputs.name: quality-scorecard
outputs.desc: Scores on completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, and uniqueness per data set

outputs.name: quality-gaps
outputs.desc: Dimensions below minimum, ranked by impact on decision-making

process: Completeness: percentage of required fields populated. Sample 100+ records.
Accuracy: verify sample against source of truth. What percentage of values are correct?
Consistency: compare same data across different systems.
Timeliness: how old is the data? Does lag exceed decision cadence?
Uniqueness: what percentage are duplicates?

steps.description: Find and fix the root cause at the source. Downstream cleaning is a bandage.

outputs.name: source-fixes
outputs.desc: Root cause at the source (input form, integration, manual process) with the fix and expected improvement

outputs.name: monitoring-setup
outputs.desc: Automated checks to catch issues before they propagate

process: Trace each gap to its source: where does data enter the system? The problem originates there.
Fix at source: completeness = required fields, accuracy = validation rules, consistency = single source of truth, timeliness = reduce pipeline lag, uniqueness = dedup at input.
Resist downstream fixes. The bad data will keep flowing.
Set up monitoring: daily completeness checks, weekly reconciliation, continuous validation.

steps.description: Run the audit quarterly. Track scores over time to verify source fixes work.

outputs.name: quarterly-report
outputs.desc: Quality scores compared to previous quarter with cause for each change

outputs.name: quality-trend
outputs.desc: Multi-quarter trend: is quality improving as source fixes accumulate?

process: Re-run scorecard quarterly with the same methodology. Compare to previous quarter.
Improved dimensions: verify the source fix is the cause. Protect it.
Degraded dimensions: investigate the new quality loss source. Apply root-cause fixing.
If quality is not improving despite fixes, monitoring is not catching new issues or fixes are not maintained.
